claim: QIL1 null alleles were identified in two siblings displaying multiple clinical symptoms of early-onset fatal mitochondrial encephalopathy with liver disease.

evidence: The claim is supported by data from whole exome sequencing and clinical observations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Patients with QIL1 null alleles have defects in respiratory chain function in muscle.

evidence: The claim is supported by respiratory chain enzyme activity measurements in patient muscle tissue.

claim: QIL1 absence in patients' fibroblasts was associated with MICOS disassembly.
source: QIL1 absence in patients' fibroblasts was associated with MICOS disassembly, abnormal cristae, mild cytochrome c oxidase defect, and sensitivity to glucose withdrawal.
evidence: The claim is supported by blue-native gel electrophoresis and quantitative proteomics data showing loss of MICOS complex assembly.

claim: QIL1 absence in patients' fibroblasts was associated with abnormal cristae.
source: QIL1 absence in patients' fibroblasts was associated with MICOS disassembly, abnormal cristae, mild cytochrome c oxidase defect, and sensitivity to glucose withdrawal.

claim: QIL1 absence in patients' fibroblasts was associated with mild cytochrome c oxidase defect.

claim: QIL1 absence in patients' fibroblasts was associated with sensitivity to glucose withdrawal.

claim: QIL1 expression rescued cristae defects in patient fibroblasts.
source: QIL1 expression rescued cristae defects, and promoted re-accumulation of MICOS subunits to facilitate MICOS assembly.
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data showing restoration of normal cristae morphology upon QIL1 expression.

claim: QIL1 expression promoted re-accumulation of MICOS subunits to facilitate MICOS assembly.
source: QIL1 expression rescued cristae defects, and promoted re-accumulation of MICOS subunits to facilitate MICOS assembly.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot and blue-native gel analysis showing increased MICOS subunit levels and complex assembly.

claim: MICOS assembly and cristae morphology were not efficiently rescued by over-expression of other MICOS subunits in patient fibroblasts.
source: MICOS assembly and cristae morphology were not efficiently rescued by over-expression of other MICOS subunits in patient fibroblasts.
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy and blue-native gel analysis of patient fibroblasts expressing various MICOS subunits.

claim: This study provides the first evidence of altered MICOS assembly linked with a human mitochondrial disease.
source: Taken together, these data provide the first evidence of altered MICOS assembly linked with a human mitochondrial disease and confirm a central role for QIL1 in stable MICOS complex formation.
evidence: The claim is based on the novel findings presented in this manuscript regarding QIL1 mutations in patients.

claim: QIL1 has a central role in stable MICOS complex formation.
source: Taken together, these data provide the first evidence of altered MICOS assembly linked with a human mitochondrial disease and confirm a central role for QIL1 in stable MICOS complex formation.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing MICOS disassembly in QIL1-deficient cells and rescue upon QIL1 expression.

claim: Proper organization of the respiratory chain within the mitochondrial inner membrane relies on the formation of cristae.
source: Proper organization of the respiratory chain and other mitochondrial protein complexes within the mitochondrial inner membrane (MIM) relies on the formation of MIM invaginations referred to as cristae.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about mitochondrial structure and function.

claim: Cristae are laminar structures with highly curved distal membrane arrangement.
source: These laminar structures with highly curved distal membrane arrangement are formed through the mitochondrial contact site (MICOS) complex, a cristae junction scaffold that is thought to both maintain close proximity of cristae membranes near the 'boundary' MIM as well as form connections between the cristae junction and the mitochondrial outer membrane (MOM) (Pfanner et al., 2014; van der Laan et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established scientific literature.

claim: MICOS is composed of several subunits located on the MIM and mitochondrial intermembrane space, including MIC25, MIC60, MIC10, MIC26, MIC27, and MIC19.

evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about MICOS composition.

claim: The MICOS core complex has been shown to interact with SAM50, MTX1, and MTX2 on the MOM.

claim: Depletion of QIL1 by RNAi resulted in loss of cristae junction structures accompanied by the formation of MIMs with characteristic 'swirl' structures.
source: Depletion of QIL1 by RNAi in tissue culture cell lines resulted in: (1) loss of cristae junction structures accompanied by the formation of MIMs with characteristic 'swirl' structures, (2) MICOS complex disassembly, (3) loss of MIC10, MIC26 and MIC27 protein levels, (4) failure to assemble into a MIC60-MIC19-MIC25 sub-complex, and (5) decreased mitochondrial respiration (Guarani et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Depletion of QIL1 by RNAi resulted in MICOS complex disassembly.
source: Depletion of QIL1 by RNAi in tissue culture cell lines resulted in: (1) loss of cristae junction structures accompanied by the formation of MIMs with characteristic 'swirl' structures, (2) MICOS complex disassembly, (3) loss of MIC10, MIC26 and MIC27 protein levels, (4) failure to assemble into a MIC60-MIC19-MIC25 sub-complex, and (5) decreased mitochondrial respiration (Guarani et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Fibroblasts from both patients displayed apparently normal overall respiration.

claim: Patient fibroblasts displayed reduced cell number 7 days after glucose withdrawal compared with control fibroblasts.
source: Compared with control fibroblasts, patient fibroblasts displayed reduced cell number 7 days after glucose withdrawal (Figure 1H), a characteristic often observed in mitochondrial disease and indicative of a limited capacity for mitochondria to respond to the metabolic challenge resulting from glycolysis limitation (Lee et al., 2014; Robinson et al., 1992; van den Heuvel et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is based on cell growth experiments shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Reduced cell number after glucose withdrawal is a characteristic often observed in mitochondrial disease.
source: Compared with control fibroblasts, patient fibroblasts displayed reduced cell number 7 days after glucose withdrawal (Figure 1H), a characteristic often observed in mitochondrial disease and indicative of a limited capacity for mitochondria to respond to the metabolic challenge resulting from glycolysis limitation (Lee et al., 2014; Robinson et al., 1992; van den Heuvel et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Reduced cell number after glucose withdrawal is indicative of a limited capacity for mitochondria to respond to the metabolic challenge resulting from glycolysis limitation.
source: Compared with control fibroblasts, patient fibroblasts displayed reduced cell number 7 days after glucose withdrawal (Figure 1H), a characteristic often observed in mitochondrial disease and indicative of a limited capacity for mitochondria to respond to the metabolic challenge resulting from glycolysis limitation (Lee et al., 2014; Robinson et al., 1992; van den Heuvel et al., 2004).

claim: Mitochondrial respiratory chain dysfunction was shown in the skeletal muscle biopsy of patient 1, which presented with deficiencies across all respiratory chain complexes.

claim: Sequence and quantification of mitochondrial DNA extracted from skeletal muscle were normal in patient 1.
source: Sequence and quantification of mitochondrial DNA extracted from skeletal muscle were normal (Patient 1: 4500 copies/cell (n = 3); Control range: 1700–6000 copies/cell [15 infants]).

claim: A homozygous mutation (c.30-1G>A) in C19orf70 (QIL1) was identified in both patients.
source: We identified a homozygous mutation (c.30-1G>A) in C19orf70 (QIL1) in both patients (Figure 2A), and this mutation was confirmed by Sanger sequencing of PCR products from patient DNA extracted from fibroblasts.
evidence: The claim is based on whole exome sequencing and Sanger sequencing data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Parents of the patients were found to be heterozygous at the QIL1 locus.
source: Parents were found to be heterozygous at this locus (Figure 2A,B), consistent with autosomal recessive transmission.
evidence: The claim is based on Sanger sequencing data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: The inheritance pattern is consistent with autosomal recessive transmission.
source: Parents were found to be heterozygous at this locus (Figure 2A,B), consistent with autosomal recessive transmission.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the genetic data showing both parents are heterozygous and both patients are homozygous.

claim: The G>A mutation in the 5' splice-donor sequence in exon 2 caused the QIL1 mRNA to contain exon 1 fused to exon 3.
source: Consistent with a G>A mutation in the 5' splice-donor sequence in exon 2, the QIL1 mRNA contained exon 1 fused to exon 3 (Figure 2C–F), which produced a frame-shift at Ser10 in the annotated QIL1 cDNA (NM_205767.2) leading directly into an alternative reading frame encoded by exon 3 and a premature stop codon (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is based on RT-PCR and sequencing data shown in Figure 2C-F.

claim: The altered QIL1 mRNA produced a frame-shift at Ser10 leading to an alternative reading frame and a premature stop codon.
source: Consistent with a G>A mutation in the 5' splice-donor sequence in exon 2, the QIL1 mRNA contained exon 1 fused to exon 3 (Figure 2C–F), which produced a frame-shift at Ser10 in the annotated QIL1 cDNA (NM_205767.2) leading directly into an alternative reading frame encoded by exon 3 and a premature stop codon (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The encoded putative protein contains only 9 residues from QIL1 and lacks the transmembrane domain.
source: Given that the encoded putative protein contains only 9 residues from QIL1 and lacks the transmembrane domain primarily derived from exon 2, we conclude that the encoded protein corresponds to a functionally null allele (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of the predicted protein sequence shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The encoded protein corresponds to a functionally null allele.
source: Given that the encoded putative protein contains only 9 residues from QIL1 and lacks the transmembrane domain primarily derived from exon 2, we conclude that the encoded protein corresponds to a functionally null allele (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the structural analysis of the mutant protein.

claim: QIL1 protein at ~11 kDa was not detected in patient fibroblasts but was abundant in control fibroblasts.
source: Consistent with production of an altered QIL1 protein, we failed to detect a band at ~11 kDa corresponding to QIL1 in patient fibroblasts, but this protein was abundant in control fibroblasts based on immunoblotting of whole-cell extracts (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is based on immunoblot data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The abundance of MIC10, MIC26, MIC27, MIC25, MIC19, and MIC60 was reduced in both patient cell lines.
source: The abundance of all six proteins was reduced in both patient cell lines, with MIC10, MIC26 and MIC27 being affected to the largest extent (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: The claim is based on immunoblot and densitometry data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: MIC10, MIC26 and MIC27 were affected to the largest extent in patient cell lines.
source: The abundance of all six proteins was reduced in both patient cell lines, with MIC10, MIC26 and MIC27 being affected to the largest extent (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: The claim is based on immunoblot and densitometry data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: QIL1 mRNA was greatly reduced in both patient cell lines relative to controls.
source: Importantly, while QIL1 mRNA was greatly reduced in both patient cell lines relative to controls, the levels of mRNA for MIC10, MIC26, and MIC27 were largely unaffected in patient cell lines (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is based on qPCR data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The levels of mRNA for MIC10, MIC26, and MIC27 were largely unaffected in patient cell lines.
source: Importantly, while QIL1 mRNA was greatly reduced in both patient cell lines relative to controls, the levels of mRNA for MIC10, MIC26, and MIC27 were largely unaffected in patient cell lines (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is based on qPCR data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Loss of MICOS subunits appears to occur through post-transcriptional mechanisms.
source: Thus, loss of MICOS subunits appears to occur through post-transcriptional mechanisms.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that protein levels are reduced while mRNA levels are normal.

claim: Severe cristae morphology abnormalities were observed in the vast majority of mitochondria in patient fibroblasts.
source: We observed severe cristae morphology abnormalities in the vast majority of mitochondria in fibroblasts, with >92% of mitochondria displaying loss of cristae structures and the appearance of characteristic 'swirl' structures similar to those previously seen upon depletion of MICOS subunits (Figure 3D) (Alkhaja et al., 2012; Guarani et al., 2015; John et al., 2005; Weber et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: >92% of mitochondria in patient fibroblasts displayed loss of cristae structures and the appearance of characteristic 'swirl' structures.
source: We observed severe cristae morphology abnormalities in the vast majority of mitochondria in fibroblasts, with >92% of mitochondria displaying loss of cristae structures and the appearance of characteristic 'swirl' structures similar to those previously seen upon depletion of MICOS subunits (Figure 3D) (Alkhaja et al., 2012; Guarani et al., 2015; John et al., 2005; Weber et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on quantitative electron microscopy analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The 'swirl' structures observed are similar to those previously seen upon depletion of MICOS subunits.
source: We observed severe cristae morphology abnormalities in the vast majority of mitochondria in fibroblasts, with >92% of mitochondria displaying loss of cristae structures and the appearance of characteristic 'swirl' structures similar to those previously seen upon depletion of MICOS subunits (Figure 3D) (Alkhaja et al., 2012; Guarani et al., 2015; John et al., 2005; Weber et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies showing similar phenotypes.

claim: Mitochondria in patient fibroblasts were enlarged and swollen, round or elongated.
source: While the majority of mitochondria in control fibroblasts were tubular in structure, mitochondria in patient fibroblasts were enlarged and swollen, round or elongated, consistent with a dramatic loss in architecture.
evidence: The claim is based on electron microscopy observations.

claim: Mitochondria in skeletal muscle from patient 1 were swollen and filled with inner membranes displaying 'swirl' structures.
source: Similarly, mitochondria in skeletal muscle from patient 1 were also swollen and filled with inner membranes displaying 'swirl' structures (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is based on electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: QIL1 expression converted abnormal mitochondria in patient cells into tubular structures with intact cristae junctions in 70–80% of cells.
source: Importantly, QIL1 expression converted abnormal mitochondria in patient cells into tubular structures with intact cristae junctions in 70–80% of cells as assessed by electron microscopy (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: The claim is based on electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: QIL1 overexpression resulted in altered cristae morphology in ~30% control neonatal fibroblasts, with mitochondria displaying hyper-branched cristae.
source: We found that QIL1 overexpression resulted in altered cristae morphology in ~30% control neonatal fibroblasts, with mitochondria displaying hyper-branched cristae, which were also termed abnormal (Figure 4A, data not shown).
evidence: The claim is based on electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: QIL1 expressing cells displayed increased levels of MIC10 and MIC60.
source: Moreover, QIL1 expressing cells displayed increased levels of MIC10 and MIC60, consistent with rescue of the biochemical defects in MICOS complex assembly (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is based on immunoblot data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Control fibroblasts contained a major MICOS complex at ~700 kDa as assessed using anti-MIC10 or anti-MIC60 antibodies.
source: As expected, control fibroblasts contained a major MICOS complex at ~700 kDa as assessed using anti-MIC10 or anti-MIC60 antibodies (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: The claim is based on blue-native gel electrophoresis data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: In patient fibroblasts lacking QIL1, MIC10 and MIC60 were lost from the ~700 kDa complex.
source: However, in patient fibroblasts lacking QIL1, MIC10 and MIC60 were lost from the ~700 kDa complex, with MIC60 found a lower abundance complex at ~500 kDa (Figure 5A,B,D).
evidence: The claim is based on blue-native gel electrophoresis data shown in Figure 5A,B,D.

claim: MIC60 was found in a lower abundance complex at ~500 kDa in patient fibroblasts.
source: However, in patient fibroblasts lacking QIL1, MIC10 and MIC60 were lost from the ~700 kDa complex, with MIC60 found a lower abundance complex at ~500 kDa (Figure 5A,B,D).
evidence: The claim is based on blue-native gel electrophoresis data shown in Figure 5A,B,D.

claim: ATP5A complexes representing Complex V of the respiratory chain were unaffected in patient samples.
source: In contrast, ATP5A complexes representing Complex V of the respiratory chain were unaffected in patient samples (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is based on blue-native gel electrophoresis data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: A marked reduction of all detected MICOS subunits at ~700 kDa was observed in patient 2 fibroblasts.
source: We observed a marked reduction of all detected MICOS subunits at ~700 kDa (Figure 5F; H:L ratio <1, green) in patient 2 fibroblasts.
evidence: The claim is based on quantitative proteomics data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The abundance of the mature heterooligomeric MICOS complex is greatly reduced in patient fibroblasts.
source: Thus, the abundance of the mature heterooligomeric complex (Harner et al., 2011; Ott et al., 2012) is greatly reduced.
evidence: The claim is based on quantitative proteomics data and supported by citations to prior work defining the mature complex.

claim: An accumulation of MIC19 and MIC60 in a smaller ~500 kDa sub-complex was observed in patient fibroblasts relative to control fibroblasts.
source: Concomitantly, we observed an accumulation of MIC19 and MIC60 in a smaller ~500 kDa sub-complex in patient fibroblasts relative to control fibroblasts (Figure 5F; H:L ratio >1, red).
evidence: The claim is based on quantitative proteomics data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Loss of QIL1 in patients leads to an overall reduction in mature MICOS and an increase in the abundance of a sub-complex containing MIC19 and MIC60.
source: These results are consistent with previous proteomic studies of QIL1-depleted cells (Guarani et al., 2015) and indicate that loss of QIL1 in patients leads to an overall reduction in mature MICOS and an increase in the abundance of a sub-complex containing MIC19 and MIC60.
evidence: The claim is based on quantitative proteomics data and supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Expression of QIL1-HA-FLAG in patient fibroblasts resulted in the rescue of MICOS complex assembly.
source: This resulted in the rescue of MICOS complex assembly as assessed using anti-MIC10 on blue-native gels (Figure 5G) as well as rescue of MIC10 levels (Figure 5I).
evidence: The claim is based on blue-native gel electrophoresis and immunoblot data shown in Figure 5G,I.

claim: QIL1-HA-FLAG rescued MIC60, MIC10, MIC19 and MIC27 levels in patient fibroblasts.
source: QIL1-HA-FLAG rescued not only MIC60 and MIC10 (Figures 4B, 5I, Figure 5—figure supplement 1N) but also MIC19 and MIC27 levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 1N), consistent with formation of MICOS.
evidence: The claim is based on immunoblot data shown in multiple figures.

claim: Expression of MIC60 and MIC19 failed to rescue QIL1-deficiency by electron microscopy or by blue-native gel analysis of MIC10 assembly into MICOS.
source: Expression of MIC60 and MIC19 failed to rescue QIL1-deficiency by electron microscopy (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F,G) or by blue-native gel analysis of MIC10 assembly into MICOS (Figure 5—figure supplement 1L).
evidence: The claim is based on electron microscopy and blue-native gel data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: MIC27 and MIC10 overexpression resulted in very low abundance MIC10 at the position of the MICOS complex in blue-native gel analysis.
source: In the case of MIC27 and MIC10 overexpression, we observed very low abundance MIC10 at the position of the MICOS complex in blue-native gel analysis, as well as additional low abundance complexes migrating at ~800 kDa and at much lower mass (~100 kDa) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1L), suggesting an ability of overexpression of these proteins (Figure 5—figure supplement 1N) to support low efficiency or possibly aberrant or alternative assembly.
evidence: The claim is based on blue-native gel electrophoresis data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1L.

claim: ~30% of individual mitochondria in QIL1-defective fibroblasts overexpressing MIC27 and MIC10 displayed mitochondria with evidence of cristae-like structures.
source: Interestingly, ~30% of individual mitochondria in QIL1-defective fibroblasts overexpressing MIC27 and MIC10 displayed mitochondria with evidence of cristae-like structures (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H,J), while the majority of mitochondria in these cells contained swirl like inner membrane structures typical of disruption of MICOS (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I,K).
evidence: The claim is based on electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1H,J.

claim: MIC27 and MIC10 overexpression has a weak ability to support cristae formation independently of QIL1.
source: These data suggest a weak ability of MIC27 and MIC10 overexpression to support cristae formation independently of QIL1 (see Discussion).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the electron microscopy and biochemical data.

claim: QIL1 deficiency was associated with transient neonatal deterioration with hypoglycemia, hyperlactacidemia and liver disease.
source: QIL1 deficiency was associated with transient neonatal deterioration with hypoglycemia, hyperlactacidemia and liver disease.
evidence: The claim is based on clinical observations documented in the manuscript.

claim: In the first months of life, acute decompensations occurred with liver disease and hyperlactacidemia in the patients.
source: In the first months of life, acute decompensations occurred with liver disease and hyperlactacidemia.
evidence: The claim is based on clinical observations documented in the manuscript.

claim: The patients had neurological disease, including developmental delay with cerebellar atrophy, eye disease with optic atrophy and sensorineural deafness.
source: This was associated with neurological disease, including developmental delay with cerebellar atrophy, eye disease with optic atrophy and sensorineural deafness.
evidence: The claim is based on clinical observations documented in the manuscript.

claim: Liver disease in the patients included liver nodules with high α-fetoprotein as observed in other mitochondrial disease such as TRMU gene mutations.
source: Liver disease also included liver nodules with high α-fetoprotein as observed in other mitochondrial disease such as TRMU gene mutations (Gaignard et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on clinical observations and supported by citation to similar findings in other mitochondrial diseases.

claim: Liver associated with central nervous system dysfunction is often involved in mitochondrial disease especially those involving defects of mitochondrial DNA maintenance.
source: Liver associated with central nervous system dysfunction is often involved in mitochondrial disease especially those involving defects of mitochondrial DNA maintenance caused by nuclear gene mutations i.e. mitochondrial DNA depletion syndromes (resulting from POLG, DGUOK or MPV17 mutations for instance (Al-Hussaini et al., 2014; Naviaux and Nguyen, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature on mitochondrial diseases.

claim: QIL1 deficiency in patient fibroblasts did not affect mitochondrial DNA abundance.
source: QIL1 deficiency in patient fibroblasts did not affect mitochondrial DNA abundance, but resulted in severely disorganized mitochondrial cristae.
evidence: The claim is based on mitochondrial DNA quantification measurements.

claim: The deletion of exon 2, which encoded the single-pass transmembrane domain, would be expected to greatly reduce the efficiency of MICOS assembly.
source: In principle, the deletion of exon 2, which encoded the single-pass transmembrane domain apparently involved in QIL1 tethering to the MIM (Figure 2), would be expected to greatly reduce the efficiency of MICOS assembly (Guarani et al., 2015; Zerbes et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from structural analysis and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The mRNA for the QIL1 mutant is likely degraded through non-sense mediated decay.
source: Given the presence of a premature stop codon in the mRNA for the QIL1 mutant, it is likely that the mRNA is degraded through non-sense mediated decay.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the presence of a premature stop codon and knowledge of mRNA quality control mechanisms.

claim: Generalized mitochondrial respiratory chain deficiencies were detected in skeletal muscle from patient 1 consistent with reduced mitochondrial respiration previously reported upon QIL1 RNAi mediated knockdown in human cell lines.
source: We also detected generalized mitochondrial respiratory chain deficiencies in skeletal muscle from patient 1 consistent with a reduced mitochondrial respiration previously reported upon QIL1 RNAi mediated knockdown in human cell lines (Guarani et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on respiratory chain enzyme measurements and supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Contrary to RNAi-induced QIL1 depletion in HeLa cells, there was no effect of QIL1 deficiency on fibroblasts' basal respiration.
source: Interestingly, contrary to what was observed in RNAi-induced QIL1 depletion in HeLa cells (Guarani et al., 2015), there was no effect of QIL1 deficiency on fibroblasts' basal respiration in agreement with the limited defect affecting complex IV and the normal respiratory chain enzyme activities in these cells.
evidence: The claim is based on oxygen consumption measurements and comparison to prior work.

claim: Differences in mitochondrial activities observed between muscle biopsies and skin fibroblasts from patients are commonly observed in mitochondrial disorders.
source: Differences in mitochondrial activities observed between muscle biopsies and skin fibroblasts from patients are commonly observed in mitochondrial disorders (Haas et al., 2008; Thorburn and Smeitink, 2001; van den Heuvel et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature on mitochondrial disorders.

claim: Nearly 50% of children with a respiratory chain defect in muscle display normal enzyme activities in cultured skin fibroblasts.
source: It has been reported that nearly 50% of the children with a respiratory chain defect in muscle display normal enzyme activities in cultured skin fibroblasts (Thorburn, 2000) and respiratory chain defects are often not expressed in fibroblasts even in some well-recognized oxidative phosphorylation deficiencies (Robinson et al., 1990).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Patients' fibroblasts exhibited high sensitivity to glucose deprivation, suggesting an inability to utilize the alternative mitochondrial energetic route to cope with glucose deprivation.
source: Nevertheless, patients' fibroblasts exhibited high sensitivity to glucose deprivation, suggesting an inability to utilize the alternative mitochondrial energetic route to cope with glucose deprivation, in line with previous observations from other mitochondrial diseases (Robinson et al., 1992).
evidence: The claim is based on cell growth experiments and supported by citation to similar findings in other mitochondrial diseases.

claim: An increase in cristae density has been reported upon general nutrient or glucose deprivation.
source: Interestingly, an increase in cristae density has been reported upon general nutrient or glucose deprivation (Gomes et al., 2011; Rossignol et al., 2004), indicating an important link between mitochondrial architecture and nutrient utilization.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: There is an important link between mitochondrial architecture and nutrient utilization.
source: Interestingly, an increase in cristae density has been reported upon general nutrient or glucose deprivation (Gomes et al., 2011; Rossignol et al., 2004), indicating an important link between mitochondrial architecture and nutrient utilization.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from cited literature.

claim: Mitochondrial cristae architecture may control nutrient utilization via different mechanisms, including electron transport chain function, nutrient import and access.
source: It has been proposed that mitochondrial cristae architecture may control nutrient utilization via different mechanisms, including electron transport chain function, nutrient import and access (Stanley et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a hypothesis in the literature.

claim: Differences between mitochondrial respiration defects observed in muscle and fibroblasts may reflect the pleiotropic nature of phenotypes of mitochondrial diseases.
source: Thus, differences between mitochondrial respiration defects observed in muscle and fibroblasts may not only reflect the pleiotropic nature of phenotypes of mitochondrial diseases, often eliciting highly tissue-specific effects (Vafai and Mootha, 2012), but also be related to cell-specific metabolic requirements and different mitochondrial pathways.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference and supported by citation.

claim: Differences between mitochondrial respiration defects observed in muscle and fibroblasts may be related to cell-specific metabolic requirements and different mitochondrial pathways.
source: Thus, differences between mitochondrial respiration defects observed in muscle and fibroblasts may not only reflect the pleiotropic nature of phenotypes of mitochondrial diseases, often eliciting highly tissue-specific effects (Vafai and Mootha, 2012), but also be related to cell-specific metabolic requirements and different mitochondrial pathways.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference.

claim: Skin fibroblasts may have developed adaptive mechanisms over time to permit normal basal respiration under culture conditions.
source: Alternatively, skin fibroblasts may have possibly developed adaptive mechanisms over time to permit normal basal respiration under culture conditions.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a possible explanation for observed differences.

claim: Loss of QIL1 leads to loss of cristae structure and reduced levels of MIC60, MIC19, MIC25, MIC10, MIC26, and MIC27.
source: A proposed model is shown in Figure 5J, wherein loss of QIL1 leads to loss of cristae structure and reduced levels of MIC60, MIC19, MIC25, MIC10, MIC26, and MIC27, with MIC10, MIC26 and MIC27 being affected to the largest extent (Figure 3A-B, Figure 5I and Figure 5—figure supplement 1N).
evidence: The claim is based on data from multiple figures showing protein levels and cristae morphology.

claim: Residual MIC60 and MIC19 could be found in an ~500 kDa complex in blue-native gels.
source: Residual MIC60 and MIC19 could be found in an ~500 kDa complex in blue-native gels using quantitative proteomics (Figure 5F,J), suggesting that this sub-complex of MICOS does not require QIL1 for assembly (Guarani et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on quantitative proteomics data shown in Figure 5F,J.

claim: The ~500 kDa sub-complex of MICOS does not require QIL1 for assembly.
source: Residual MIC60 and MIC19 could be found in an ~500 kDa complex in blue-native gels using quantitative proteomics (Figure 5F,J), suggesting that this sub-complex of MICOS does not require QIL1 for assembly (Guarani et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data and supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The ability of MIC10 and MIC27 overexpression to promote cristae formation with low efficiency may relate to the ability of MIC10 to form large oligomers and promote membrane curvature independently of other MICOS subunits.
source: The ability of MIC10 and MIC27 overexpression to promote cristae formation with low efficiency may relate to the ability of MIC10 to form large oligomers and promote membrane curvature independently of other MICOS subunits (Barbot et al., 2015; Bohnert et al., 2015) and MIC27 to bind cardiolipin which also promotes curvature (Weber et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: MIC27 binds cardiolipin which promotes membrane curvature.
source: The ability of MIC10 and MIC27 overexpression to promote cristae formation with low efficiency may relate to the ability of MIC10 to form large oligomers and promote membrane curvature independently of other MICOS subunits (Barbot et al., 2015; Bohnert et al., 2015) and MIC27 to bind cardiolipin which also promotes curvature (Weber et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: MIC27 expression increased MIC10 levels.
source: Interestingly, we observed that MIC27 expression increased MIC10 levels, and it is possible that the ability of MIC27 to support complex formation with low efficiency may reflect stabilization of MIC10 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1L,N).
evidence: The claim is based on immunoblot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1L,N.

claim: The ability of MIC27 to support complex formation with low efficiency may reflect stabilization of MIC10.
source: Interestingly, we observed that MIC27 expression increased MIC10 levels, and it is possible that the ability of MIC27 to support complex formation with low efficiency may reflect stabilization of MIC10 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1L,N).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the data.

claim: MIC27 expression positively correlates with the levels of MIC10.
source: These findings are in line with previous observations by Koob et al who reported that MIC27 expression positively correlated with the levels of MIC10, and proposed that MIC26 and MIC27 modulate MIC10 levels (Koob et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: MIC26 and MIC27 modulate MIC10 levels.
source: These findings are in line with previous observations by Koob et al who reported that MIC27 expression positively correlated with the levels of MIC10, and proposed that MIC26 and MIC27 modulate MIC10 levels (Koob et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a hypothesis in prior work.

claim: MIC27 promotes the stability of the MIC10 oligomers.
source: Zerbes at al also reported that MIC27 promotes the stability of the MIC10 oligomers (Zerbes et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Fibroblasts from patients have highly enlarged mitochondrial structures, suggesting loss of appropriate mitochondrial fission-fusion cycles.
source: Additionally, we note that fibroblasts from patients have highly enlarged mitochondrial structures, suggesting loss of appropriate mitochondrial fission-fusion cycles, and the absence of mitophagic destruction of damaged mitochondria.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from electron microscopy observations.

claim: Patient fibroblasts show absence of mitophagic destruction of damaged mitochondria.
source: Additionally, we note that fibroblasts from patients have highly enlarged mitochondrial structures, suggesting loss of appropriate mitochondrial fission-fusion cycles, and the absence of mitophagic destruction of damaged mitochondria.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from electron microscopy observations.

claim: Similar defects in fusion-fission cycles and development of swollen mitochondria have been observed in cells lacking the MICOS subunit MIC60.
source: Similar defects in fusion-fission cycles and development of swollen mitochondria has been observed in cells lacking the MICOS subunit MIC60, suggesting that the observed phenotype is a general property of disruption of cristae structures (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The observed phenotype is a general property of disruption of cristae structures.
source: Similar defects in fusion-fission cycles and development of swollen mitochondria has been observed in cells lacking the MICOS subunit MIC60, suggesting that the observed phenotype is a general property of disruption of cristae structures (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from comparison to prior work.

claim: Both patients examined have persistent urinary excretion of 3-methylglutaconic acid that might be ascribed to mitochondrial cristae disassembly.
source: An additional interesting feature of both patients examined here is persistent urinary excretion of 3-methylglutaconic acid that might also be ascribed to mitochondrial cristae disassembly (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the biochemical findings.

claim: 3-methylglutaconic aciduria is observed in other mitochondrial diseases, most specifically in genetic defects of phospholipid biosynthesis, remodeling and metabolism.
source: 3-methylglutaconic aciduria is observed in other mitochondrial diseases, but most specifically in a new category of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial-related diseases, namely genetic defects of phospholipid biosynthesis, remodeling and metabolism (Garcia-Cazorla et al., 2015; Lu and Claypool, 2015; Mayr, 2015; Wortmann et al., 2013, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Primary defects in mitochondrial inner membrane cristae architecture as observed with QIL1 deficiency cause severe mitochondrial disease in humans clinically indistinguishable from primary oxidative phosphorylation respiratory chain disease.
source: In conclusion, this report demonstrates that primary defects in mitochondrial inner membrane cristae architecture as observed with QIL1 deficiency causes severe mitochondrial disease in human clinically indistinguishable from primary oxidative phosphorylation respiratory chain disease.
evidence: The claim is based on the clinical and molecular findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: This is the first report of early onset fatal mitochondrial encephalopathy in patients with mutations in a core MICOS complex subunit.
source: This is also the first report of early onset fatal mitochondrial encephalopathy in patients with mutations in a core MICOS complex subunit.
evidence: The claim is based on the novel findings presented in this manuscript.

claim: CHCHD10 haploinsufficiency demonstrates impaired MICOS complex stability, cristae formation and mitochondrial genome organization.
source: CHCHD10 haploinsufficiency, found in a family with neurodegenerative disorders and mitochondrial respiratory chain defects also demonstrates impaired MICOS complex stability, cristae formation and mitochondrial genome organization (Genin et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Alterations of different MICOS subunit protein levels and amino acid substitutions have been associated with diabetic cardiomyopathy, neurodegeneration and cancer in cellular and animal model systems.
source: Noticeably, alterations of different MICOS subunit protein levels and amino acid substitutions have been associated with several conditions, such as diabetic cardiomyopathy, neurodegeneration and cancer in cellular and animal model systems (Zerbes et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: QIL1 and other MICOS subunits represent potential candidates for mutations in patients with unexplained early onset neurological deterioration with optic and cerebellar atrophy progressing over time combined with liver disease and 3-methylglutaconic aciduria.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that QIL1 and other MICOS subunits represent potential candidates for mutations in patients with unexplained early onset neurological deterioration with optic and cerebellar atrophy progressing over time combined with liver disease and 3-methylglutaconic aciduria.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the findings in this manuscript.
